metadata.title: Prediction Markets to Let Users Bet on Coinbase, Robinhood and Marathon Targets

content.text:
The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission has approved a Cboe Global Markets plan to list binary options tied to key performance indicators for a select group of publicly traded companies, giving traders a way to bet on figures such as Coinbase's trading volume, Robinhood's customer count and MARA's bitcoin production.
The decision drew little attention in a week when traders were focused on bitcoin trading above $80,000 around key U.S. inflation data. A binary option is the simplest options contract, letting traders bet on a yes-or-no question, such as whether Coinbase's trading volume will exceed a set number by a specific date.

SEC Chairman Paul Atkins approved the rule change Cboe filed, according to a statement dated Oct. 13. The contracts are cash-settled and European-style, meaning they can be exercised only at expiration, and they will settle on figures in companies' SEC filings rather than numbers in earnings presentations.
The metrics include trading volume at Coinbase (NASDAQ: $COIN), customer count and revenue at Robinhood Markets (NASDAQ: $HOOD), and bitcoin production at MARA Holdings (NASDAQ: $MARA). Eleanor Terrett, host of Crypto America, said on X that the contracts give crypto traders a new way to bet on the performance of crypto-linked companies without wagering directly on bitcoin's price. She noted that the SEC approved this specific securities-options structure while leaving room for differently structured contracts to fall under the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.
Cboe plans to list the contracts this month, and Robinhood is expected to be the first brokerage to offer them to retail investors. Cboe and Robinhood announced the plan Sept. 30 at Robinhood's HOOD Summit and said both would waive fees through the end of 2026. Trading cannot begin until the clearing house, Cboe Clear U.S., receives provisional registration, and a separate application is pending.
Atkins said the approval does not affect similar contracts overseen by the CFTC, such as those on prediction market platform Kalshi. He said turf fights between the agencies have hindered innovation for decades, and that the approval "reflects a new spirit of harmony, innovation, and investor choice."
